questions.q: What will `printf` output when accessing `p[1][2]` via a pointer to array `int (*p)[3]`?
questions.hint: Does `p[1]` point to the second row of the array (`{4, 5, 6}`)?
explanations: Correct! The declaration `int (*p)[3]` creates a pointer to an array of 3 integers. Expression `p[1]` selects the second row `{4, 5, 6}`, and index `[2]` takes its third element — 6.
Incorrect. 5 is element `p[1][1]`.
Incorrect. 3 is an element of the first row `p[0][2]`.
Incorrect. 2 is element `p[0][1]`.

questions.topic: Matrices — Linear Addressing i * cols + j
questions.q: What is expression `p[1 * cols + 1]` equal to when linearly reading a `2x3` matrix via a 1D pointer?
questions.hint: Which element of 2D matrix `m[i][j]` is at linear index 4?
explanations: Correct! Matrix memory stores rows sequentially (row-major order). Index $1 \times 3 + 1 = 4$ corresponds to the 5th element of the contiguous memory block: `m[0][0]` (10), `m[0][1]` (20), `m[0][2]` (30), `m[1][0]` (40), `m[1][1]` (50).
Incorrect. 40 is at index 3 (`m[1][0]`).
Incorrect. 20 is at index 1 (`m[0][1]`).
Incorrect. 60 is at index 5 (`m[1][2]`).

questions.q: What will `printf("%d", *arr[1])` output for an array of pointers `int *arr[3] = {&x, &y, &z}`?
questions.hint: Which address is stored in `arr[1]` and what is its value upon dereferencing `*`?
explanations: Correct! Declaration `int *arr[3]` creates an array of 3 pointers. Element `arr[1]` contains the address of variable `y`. The dereference operator `*arr[1]` retrieves the value of `y`, which is 20.
Incorrect. 10 is the value of `*arr[0]` (variable `x`).
Incorrect. 30 is the value of `*arr[2]` (variable `z`).
Incorrect. Arrays of pointers are completely valid in C.

questions.topic: sizeof Operator — Size of Entire Matrix and Size of One Row
questions.q: What will `printf` output for `sizeof(a)` and `sizeof(a[0])` of matrix `int a[3][4]` given a 4-byte `int`?
questions.hint: Calculate the total size of the entire $3 \times 4$ element matrix and the size of one row of 4 elements.
explanations: Correct! The entire matrix contains $3 \times 4 = 12$ elements of 4 bytes each, giving $12 \times 4 = 48$ bytes. Element `a[0]` is a row of 4 integers, occupying $4 \times 4 = 16$ bytes. Output: `48 16`.
Incorrect. 12 and 4 are element counts, not sizes in bytes.
Incorrect. 4 bytes is the size of only a single `int` element, not the whole row `a[0]`.
Incorrect. Recalculate the size of the entire matrix carefully.

questions.q: What is expression `(*(a + 1))[0]` equal to for matrix `int a[2][2] = {{5, 10}, {15, 20}}`?
questions.hint: Which row does expression `*(a + 1)` select?
explanations: Correct! Expression `*(a + 1)` gets the subarray of the second row (`a[1]`). Applying index `[0]` reads its first element `a[1][0]`, which is 15.
Incorrect. 5 is element `(*(a + 0))[0]` (`a[0][0]`).
Incorrect. 10 is element `(*(a + 0))[1]` (`a[0][1]`).
Incorrect. 20 is element `(*(a + 1))[1]` (`a[1][1]`).

questions.q: What will variable `sum` equal after passing through the loop over diagonal `a[i][i]`?
questions.hint: Add up the elements located at the intersection of identical rows and columns: (0,0), (1,1), (2,2).
explanations: Correct! Expression `a[i][i]` accesses main diagonal elements of the matrix: `a[0][0]` (1), `a[1][1]` (2), and `a[2][2]` (3). Sum equals $1 + 2 + 3 = 6$.
Incorrect. Off-diagonal elements equal 0, but on the diagonal itself are numbers 1, 2, and 3.
Incorrect. 3 is only the last diagonal element.
Incorrect. Recalculate the sum of all three elements.

questions.topic: Dynamic Memory — Allocating a 2D Matrix via int **
questions.q: What is element `m[1][0]` equal to for a dynamically created 2D structure?
questions.hint: Was value 42 successfully assigned to the first cell of the second row?
explanations: Correct! Code creates an array of pointers `m`, where each pointer stores its own dynamic 1D `int` array. Operation `m[1][0] = 42` correctly writes value into the second row and outputs 42.
Incorrect. Value 42 was explicitly written over uninitialized memory.
Incorrect. Variable received value 42 before output.
Incorrect. Creating dynamic matrices via `int**` is a classic C pattern.

questions.topic: String Arrays — Size of 2D Character Array char a[N][M]
questions.q: What is `sizeof(a)` equal to for 2D character array `char a[2][10]`?
questions.hint: How many `char` elements in total are allocated in memory regardless of written string lengths?
explanations: Correct! 2D array `char a[2][10]` allocates a contiguous memory block for exactly $2 \times 10 = 20$ `char` elements. Since `sizeof(char) == 1`, total size equals 20 bytes.
Incorrect. 5 is total character count in phrases "hi" and "bye".
Incorrect. 16 bytes would be occupied by an array of pointers `char *a[2]` on a 64-bit system.
Incorrect. 8 bytes is occupied by a regular pointer.

questions.topic: Memory — Casting Matrix Type to Flat Pointer (int*)a
questions.q: What will `printf` output when examining first `p[0]` and last `p[3]` elements of a `2x2` matrix via flat pointer?
questions.hint: In what order are elements of matrix `{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}` placed in contiguous memory?
explanations: Correct! In memory, elements of `2x2` matrix lie strictly sequentially: index 0: `a[0][0]` (1), index 1: `a[0][1]` (2), index 2: `a[1][0]` (3), index 3: `a[1][1]` (4). `p[0]` equals 1, and `p[3]` equals 4.
Incorrect. 1 and 2 are elements of first row `p[0]` and `p[1]`.
Incorrect. 1 and 3 are elements `p[0]` and `p[2]`.
Incorrect. Check order of elements in memory.

questions.topic: Function Parameters — Passing 2D Array int m[][N]
questions.q: What will function `print_val` output when matrix `a[2][3]` is passed to it?
questions.hint: Which element of original matrix `a` corresponds to index `m[1][1]`?
explanations: Correct! When passing a matrix to a function, specifying second dimension `[][3]` is required. Element `m[1][1]` references second row and second column of matrix, which is number 5.
Incorrect. 4 is element `m[1][0]`.
Incorrect. 2 is element `m[0][1]`.
Incorrect. 6 is element `m[1][2]`.

questions.q: What is element `a[1][0][1]` equal to in 3D array `int a[2][2][2]`?
questions.hint: Step 1: select block [1]. Step 2: select row [0] of this block. Step 3: take element [1].
explanations: Correct! Index `a[1]` selects second 2D block `{{5, 6}, {7, 8}}`. Index `[0]` takes first row `{5, 6}` from it. Index `[1]` takes second element of this row — 6.
Incorrect. 5 is element `a[1][0][0]`.
Incorrect. 2 is element of first block `a[0][0][1]`.
Incorrect. 7 is element `a[1][1][0]`.

questions.topic: Initialization — Incomplete Row Initialization of Matrix
questions.q: What will `printf` output for elements `a[0][1]` and `a[1][2]` when declaring `int a[2][3] = {{1}, {4, 5}}`?
questions.hint: What replaces omitted elements in matrix rows during initialization in curly braces?
explanations: Correct! If not all elements are specified for a subarray (row), remaining slots are automatically zero-filled. First row becomes `{1, 0, 0}`, second `{4, 5, 0}`. Values `a[0][1]` and `a[1][2]` equal 0.
Incorrect. 1 is element `a[0][0]`, and 5 is `a[1][1]`.
Incorrect. `a[1][2]` also equals 0 because third cell of second row is omitted.
Incorrect. Explicit initialization guarantees absence of garbage.

questions.q: What is expression `**(a + 1)` equal to for matrix `int a[2][3] = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}}`?
questions.hint: Which row does first dereference `*(a + 1)` yield and which element does second `*` return?
explanations: Correct! Expression `a + 1` shifts pointer to 2nd row of matrix. First dereference `*(a + 1)` converts type to pointer to first element of this row (`&a[1][0]`). Second dereference `**(a + 1)` retrieves value of `a[1][0]`, which is 4.
Incorrect. 1 is element `**a` (`a[0][0]`).
Incorrect. 2 is element `*(*a + 1)` (`a[0][1]`).
Incorrect. 5 is element `*(*(a + 1) + 1)` (`a[1][1]`).

questions.q: What is expression `*(*(a) + 2)` equal to for matrix `int a[2][3] = {{10, 20, 30}, {40, 50, 60}}`?
questions.hint: Which matrix element `a[i][j]` does this notation correspond to?
explanations: Correct! Expression `*(a)` is shorthand for `*(a + 0)`, which is first row `a[0]`. Adding `+ 2` gives address of 3rd element of this row (`&a[0][2]`). Dereferencing retrieves 30.
Incorrect. 20 is element `*(*(a) + 1)` (`a[0][1]`).
Incorrect. 60 is element of 3rd column of second row `*(*(a + 1) + 2)` (`a[1][2]`).
Incorrect. 10 is initial element `**a` (`a[0][0]`).

questions.q: Is dynamic VLA matrix dimension `int a[n][m]` legal and will `a[1][2]` output value 99 in C99+?
questions.hint: Does C99 standard support dynamic VLA allocation on stack?
explanations: Correct! C99 standard allows variable length arrays (VLAs). Dimensions `n` and `m` are calculated at runtime, and assignment `a[1][2] = 99` correctly outputs 99.
Incorrect. An error would occur only in older C89 standard.
Incorrect. Working with VLAs is fully regulated in C99.
Incorrect. Cell value was explicitly changed to 99.

questions.q: What will `printf` output when initializing array via `[2] = 10, 20`?
questions.hint: From which index does array filling continue after specifying explicit index `[2]`?
explanations: Correct! In C99, initializer `[2] = 10` sets `a[2] = 10`. Next unindexed element (`20`) is written to next position `a[3]`. Unspecified elements (`a[0]`, `a[1]`, `a[4]`) are zeroed. Element `a[1]` equals 0, and `a[3]` equals 20.
Incorrect. `a[1]` remained explicitly uninitialized, taking value 0.
Incorrect. 10 was written to `a[2]`, not `a[3]`.
Incorrect. Designated initializers are standardized in C99.

questions.q: What will `printf("%d %d", p.x, p.y)` output when using explicit fields `.y = 5, .x = 10`?
questions.hint: Does initialization order depend on declaration order of fields in struct?
explanations: Correct! Designated initializers `.field` in C99 allow populating struct fields in any order. `p.x` receives value 10, and `p.y` — value 5.
Incorrect. `p.x` corresponds to passed `.x = 10`.
Incorrect. All specified fields are successfully initialized.
Incorrect. Syntax is completely correct for C99.

questions.q: What is `sizeof(struct Flex)` equal to for a struct with a flexible array `int data[]` at end?
questions.hint: Does operator `sizeof` account for size of elements of flexible array `data[]`?
explanations: Correct! In C99, flexible array member at struct end (`int data[]`) does not increase size of struct itself when calling `sizeof`. Only field `len` (4 bytes on 32/64-bit systems) plus alignment is accounted for.
Incorrect. Struct contains at least fixed field `int len`.
Incorrect. Alignment does not require additional 4 bytes for single `int`.
Incorrect. Flexible arrays are a standard C99 feature.

questions.topic: C99 — Evaluating sizeof for VLA at Runtime
questions.q: What is expression `sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0])` equal to for VLA array `int a[n]` given `n = 5`?
questions.hint: Is `sizeof` evaluated at runtime for variable length arrays in C99?
explanations: Correct! Unlike regular arrays where `sizeof` is evaluated at compile time, for VLAs in C99 it is evaluated at runtime. Total byte size $5 \times \text{sizeof(int)}$ divided by $\text{sizeof(int)}$ yields exactly 5.
Incorrect. Size of VLA array is dynamically calculated correctly.
Incorrect. `sizeof` for VLA does not return 0.
Incorrect. Expression is completely valid.

questions.topic: Qualifiers — Pointer to Constant const int *p
questions.q: What will `printf("%d", *p)` output when indirectly reading `x` via `const int *p` if variable `x` itself was modified directly (`x = 20`)?
questions.hint: Does `const int *p` forbid modifying value of original variable `x` directly via its own name?
explanations: Correct! Declaration `const int *p` only forbids modifying value *via pointer* `p` (`*p = ...` will cause error). Modifying variable `x` directly is allowed, and pointer `p` sees updated value 20.
Incorrect. 10 is old value prior to writing.
Incorrect. Modifying regular non-const object `x` is legal.
Incorrect. There is no undefined behavior here.

questions.topic: C99 — Function snprintf and Its Return Value
questions.q: What will `res` and `strlen(buf)` output when calling `snprintf(buf, 5, "Hello, World!")`?
questions.hint: What does `snprintf` return: number of actually written bytes or number of bytes that WOULD HAVE BEEN written without limits?
explanations: Correct! According to C99 standard, `snprintf` returns number of characters that WOULD HAVE BEEN written (13 without null terminator). Into buffer of size 5 fit 4 characters + null terminator `\0` ("Hell\0"), so `strlen(buf)` equals 4.
Incorrect. 4 would be returned if `snprintf` returned count of actually written characters.
Incorrect. `res` is not equal to buffer size.
Incorrect. String length in buffer excluding null terminator equals 4.

questions.topic: C99 — Variable Declarations in for Loop (Block Scope)
questions.q: What will code output given two variables `i` (outer and inside `for` block)?
questions.hint: Does variable from `for(int i = ...)` shadow same-named outer variable?
explanations: Correct! Variable `i` declared inside `for` header is visible only inside loop body. It shadows outer `i`. Inside loop 10 is printed, and after completion outer `i` remains equal to 0.
Incorrect. Outer `i` does not change during loop execution.
Incorrect. Variables have different values.
Incorrect. Declaring variable inside `for` is permitted starting from C99.

questions.q: What is value of `(int)b` equal to when assigning `_Bool b = 100`?
questions.hint: What value does any non-zero number turn into when cast to `_Bool` type?
explanations: Correct! According to C99, converting any non-zero scalar value to `_Bool` type always yields 1. Cast `(int)b` will return 1.
Incorrect. `_Bool` stores only 0 or 1.
Incorrect. 0 is obtained only when assigning zero value.
Incorrect. Overflow like with `char` does not occur here.

questions.topic: Qualifiers — Constant Pointer int * const p
questions.q: What will `printf("%d", a)` output after executing `*p = 30` via constant pointer `int * const p`?
questions.hint: What is constant in `int * const p`: address in pointer itself or data it points to?
explanations: Correct! Writing `int * const p` means pointer `p` itself is constant (cannot change address it points to). However data `*p` can be modified, so `a` becomes equal to 30.
Incorrect. 10 was initial value.
Incorrect. Error would occur only when attempting `p = &b`.
Incorrect. Modifying dereferenced constant pointer is completely legal.

questions.topic: Pointers — Subscripting Relative to Shifted Pointer p[2]
questions.q: What is value `p[2]` equal to if `p = &a[1]` for array `a = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}`?
questions.hint: Which expression `*(p + 2)` relative to original array is `p[2]` equivalent to?
explanations: Correct! Since `p` points to `a[1]` (value 2), `p[0]` is `a[1]`, `p[1]` is `a[2]`, and `p[2]` is `a[3]`, whose value equals 4.
Incorrect. 3 is `p[1]` (`a[2]`).
Incorrect. 2 is `p[0]` (`a[1]`).
Incorrect. 5 is `p[3]` (`a[4]`).

questions.topic: Preprocessor — Side Effects of Repeated Argument Evaluation in Macros
questions.q: What will `printf("%d %d", x, y)` output for `MAX(x++, y++)` with initial `x = 2, y = 3`?
questions.hint: Expand macro `((x++) > (y++) ? (x++) : (y++))` and count number of increments.
explanations: Correct! Macro expands to `((x++) > (y++) ? (x++) : (y++))`. First 2 and 3 are compared: `x` becomes 3, `y` becomes 4. Since condition is false, branch `(y++)` is executed: value 4 is selected and `y` is incremented second time to 5. Result: `x = 3, y = 5`.
Incorrect. `y` was incremented twice, not once.
Incorrect. `x++` was evaluated only once in condition.
Incorrect. Side effects took effect.

questions.q: What is keyword `restrict` added in C99 standard used for?
questions.hint: What guarantee does programmer give to compiler regarding pointer aliasing?
options: Guarantees object is accessible only through given pointer (for optimizations)
Forbids modifying memory pointed to by pointer
Automatically frees memory upon function exit
explanations: Correct! Qualifier `restrict` informs compiler that during lifetime of given pointer no other pointer will access same memory region (no pointer aliasing), allowing compiler to perform aggressive register optimizations.
Incorrect. `restrict` is not related to multithreading.
Incorrect. Forbidding memory modification is specified with `const` keyword.
Incorrect. Memory management remains manual.

questions.q: What will `printf("%d", c + 1)` output for `unsigned char c = 255`?
questions.hint: To which type is `unsigned char` automatically promoted when participating in arithmetic operations?
explanations: Correct! Due to Integer Promotions rule, types smaller than `int` (`char`, `short`) are automatically promoted to signed `int` before performing arithmetic operations. Result $255 + 1 = 256$ without `unsigned char` overflow.
Incorrect. 0 would occur if result were immediately truncated back to `unsigned char`.
Incorrect. Number does not overflow into signed negative.
Incorrect. Addition with 1 was executed.

questions.q: What will `printf("%d", 2[a])` output for array `int a[3] = {10, 20, 30}`?
questions.hint: What does expression `i[a]` turn into according to C language rules?
explanations: Correct! In C, notation `a[i]` is translated by compiler as `*(a + i)`. Since addition is commutative, `*(2 + a)` is fully equivalent to `2[a]` and returns `a[2]`, which is 30.
Incorrect. 20 is element `1[a]` (`a[1]`).
Incorrect. 10 is element `0[a]` (`a[0]`).
Incorrect. Syntax `N[arr]` is completely legal in C.

questions.q: In which C standard were single-line comments `//` officially introduced?
questions.hint: Previously this comment style was part of C++ standard, while C89 had only `/* ... */`.
explanations: Correct! Single-line comments like `//` were borrowed from C++ and officially added to C language standard in C99. In C89/C90 only multi-line comments `/* ... */` were allowed.
Incorrect. In C89/C90 `//` comments were a compilation error (or treated as compiler extension).
Incorrect. In C11 they had already been present for a long time.
Incorrect. In classic K&R C `//` comments did not exist.
